new_statements.quote: A word is bordered by word juncture (which is characterized by potential pause) and marked by primary stress on the ultima. Word juncture is represented by space. Primary stress is characterized by volume, usually on the lowest pitch level of the speaker, but varying with the type of intonation contour. It is perhaps best described as a low push. Secondary stress accompanied by a rise in pitch occurs on long vowels. Because of its length and higher pitch characteristics, it sounds, to American ears hearing it for the first time, like primary stress.
new_statements.citation: Whittle, Claudia & Ruth Lusted. 1963. Interaction of [coexistent] phonemic systems in Atta (Northern Cagayan Negrito). In Elmer Wolfenden (ed.), Papers on Philippine Languages No. 1, 26-39. Manila: Institute for Language Teaching (University of the Philippines) & Summer Institute of Linguistics.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word carries primary stress on its final syllable (the ultima), realized as loudness on a low pitch; the phonological word is delimited by word juncture (potential pause). Long vowels, which are lexically contrastive (a, i, u short vs. long; e, o always long), carry a secondary stress with a pitch rise wherever they occur, so a word like ba:ka 'cow' has high-pitched secondary prominence on the long penult and primary (low-pitch) stress on the ultima.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress, accompanied by a rise in pitch, occurs on every long vowel; it sounds like primary stress to American ears (p. 28). Spanish loans keep their source-stressed vowel as a long vowel with secondary stress and high pitch (vaca > ba:ka, banco > ba:ngku, p. 38).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for native words. Loanwords: vowels stressed in Spanish become long (secondary-stressed) vowels; pasear (Spanish final stress) > passia:r with a long final vowel (p. 38-39).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the domain is explicitly the word bordered by word juncture; forms are citation forms and examples from a corpus gathered over about four years with two named informants. Pitch of primary stress varies with intonation contour. Caveat for the catalog: because the authors' 'primary stress' is a low-pitch push on the ultima while long vowels carry high-pitched secondary prominence, a modern analyst might reinterpret the system as length-driven (weight-sensitive) prominence plus a final word-boundary marker; the source itself states fixed-final primary stress and that is what is recorded here.
new_statements.identity_note: Whittle & Lusted 1963 state explicitly that Atta has three dialects (Allacapan, Marag, Pamplona) and that the paper describes the Pamplona dialect, i.e. Pamplona Atta = pamp1244 exactly (SIL subject language att). Faire Atta (fair1238) and Pudtol Atta (pudt1237) are separate Glottolog languages; the paper's Allacapan and Marag dialects are distinguished only by final-stop treatment and are not mapped to those codes here.

sources.note: Sec. 2.1 p. 28: a word is marked by primary stress on the ultima (realized as volume on a low pitch, 'a low push'); secondary stress with a pitch rise occurs on long vowels and sounds like primary stress to English ears. Vowel length contrastive on a, i, u (p. 30, 37-38); Spanish penult-stressed vowels borrowed as long vowels with secondary stress + high pitch (p. 38); stress/length/word intonation listed as host-language features resisting loan influence (p. 39).
